sections.heading: What is paracetamol and how does it work?
sections.body:
The NHS describes paracetamol as a painkiller that is also used for a high temperature. It is used to ease pain. Paracetamol is sold in pharmacies and shops, and some types are only available on prescription. The NHS lists tablets and capsules, a liquid, tablets that are swallowed whole and dissolvable tablets.

The NHS says paracetamol seems to work by blocking chemical messengers in the brain that tell the body it is in pain. It also lowers a high temperature. A dose can take up to an hour to start working, and the effect lasts for some hours. The NHS says paracetamol can be taken with or without food, and that people can eat and drink normally while taking it. Too much paracetamol can damage the liver, according to the NHS.

Paracetamol is also one ingredient in some combined painkillers, such as co-codamol, which pairs it with codeine. The NHS says other medicines containing paracetamol, such as some cold and flu remedies, should not be taken alongside it because of the risk of overdose.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of paracetamol?
sections.body:
The NHS says serious side effects of paracetamol are rare. The main serious ones are an allergic reaction, liver problems and a problem with blood cells. A swollen throat or tongue, a raised and itchy rash, or difficulty breathing can be signs of a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), and NHS 111 Wales says to call 999 or go to A&E. Feeling sick and yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes can be signs of liver problems, and yellowing may be harder to notice on black or brown skin. Easy bruising or nosebleeds can be signs of a problem with blood cells. A leaflet for a UK paracetamol brand advises contacting a doctor about unexpected bruising or bleeding.

Taking an extra dose is unlikely to cause problems, the NHS says, but it advises getting medical advice because too much can sometimes damage the liver.

sections.heading: Taking paracetamol with other medicines or alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says paracetamol should not be taken with other medicines that contain paracetamol, because of the risk of overdose. UK product information says that metoclopramide and domperidone make paracetamol be absorbed faster. It also lists alcohol and some other medicines, such as barbiturates and tricyclic antidepressants, as things that may raise the risk of liver harm, especially after an overdose.

Product information also says that prolonged regular use of paracetamol may enhance the effect of warfarin and related anticoagulants, raising the risk of bleeding, while occasional doses have no significant effect. NHS 111 Wales advises people who take warfarin to check with a doctor or pharmacist, because regular paracetamol can raise the risk of bleeding.

On alcohol, the NHS says drinking a small amount is usually acceptable with paracetamol. It adds that drinking may not be suitable for people with some conditions, such as liver problems.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and for how long can it be used?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults can take paracetamol, but it is not suitable for everyone. It lists people who have had an allergic reaction to it, people with kidney or liver conditions, and people who drink alcohol heavily or binge drink. NHS 111 Wales advises people with a low body weight to check with a doctor or pharmacist, and the NHS says a lower dose may be needed.

NHS 111 Wales says paracetamol can be taken during pregnancy and while breastfeeding at the recommended amount. It also says there is no good evidence that paracetamol reduces fertility in men or women.

The NHS says paracetamol can be taken regularly for many years if the recommended amount is not exceeded. For short-term self-treatment, the NHS says it should not be used for more than a few days unless a doctor advises it.

faqs.q: Can paracetamol be taken with or without food?
faqs.a: The NHS says paracetamol can be taken with or without food, and that people can eat and drink normally while taking it. A dose can take up to an hour to start working. The NHS lists tablets that are swallowed whole, dissolvable tablets, capsules and a liquid.

faqs.q: What happens if too much paracetamol is taken?
faqs.a: The NHS says an extra dose is unlikely to cause problems, but too much can sometimes damage the liver, so it advises getting medical advice. It advises calling NHS 111 if more has been taken than the packet or leaflet says, even if the person feels well. NHS hospital leaflets say many people feel well in the early stages of an overdose. If told to go to A&E, the NHS says not to drive there: ask someone else to drive, or call 999 for an ambulance.

faqs.q: Can paracetamol be taken for a long time?
faqs.a: The NHS says paracetamol can be taken regularly for many years if the recommended amount is not exceeded. For short-term self-treatment, the NHS says it should not be used for more than a few days unless a doctor advises it. Some types are only available on prescription. The NHS also says it is not suitable for people who drink alcohol heavily, and that people with a low body weight may need a lower dose.

faqs.q: Is paracetamol suitable in pregnancy or when trying for a baby?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales says there is no good evidence that paracetamol reduces fertility in men or women. It also says paracetamol can be taken during pregnancy and breastfeeding at recommended amounts. The NHS says most adults can take paracetamol, but it is not suitable for everyone, including people who have had an allergic reaction to it or who have kidney or liver conditions.
